conflicts/taiping-rebellion/name: The Taiping Rebellion and Hong Xiuquan's Heavenly Kingdom
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/religionRole: The movement grew out of Hong Xiuquan's visionary reading of Protestant tracts, and its organisation, laws, calendar, iconoclasm and claim to rule were all grounded in a new religion that drew on the Bible while proclaiming Hong as God's second son. Jonathan Spence and Thomas Reilly treat that faith as the movement's core; Reilly argues the Taiping saw the Qing emperor's claims as blasphemy against God. Marxist historiography in China emphasised class struggle and peasant revolution, and others stress Han resentment of Manchu rule, the dislocation after the Opium War, overpopulation and Hakka–Punti ethnic conflict in Guangxi. Whether Taiping belief should be called Christian is debated: missionaries who visited Nanjing judged it heretical. Religion was nonetheless the central organising cause.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/sides/0/fait: Taiping religion, a heterodox movement drawing on Protestant Christianity
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/sides/1/name: Qing Empire and the regional armies
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/sides/1/lead: Empress Dowager Cixi and Prince Gong
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/sides/2/lead: British and French commanders at Shanghai
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/summary: The bloodiest civil war of the nineteenth century, launched by Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate who believed himself the younger brother of Jesus Christ, sent to destroy the 'demons' of idolatry and Manchu rule. From 1853 to 1864 his Heavenly Kingdom ruled much of the Yangzi valley from Nanjing. Its suppression by Qing regional armies, with Western assistance, cost probably 20 to 30 million lives.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/story:
Hong Xiuquan (1814–1864) was a Hakka from Hua county near Guangzhou who repeatedly failed the imperial civil-service examinations. In 1836 he was handed Good Words to Exhort the Age, a set of tracts by Liang Fa, the first Chinese Protestant evangelist, who had worked with the missionaries Robert Morrison and William Milne. After his third failure in 1837 Hong fell ill and experienced visions in which he ascended to heaven, met a venerable father with a golden beard and an elder brother, and was commissioned to slay demons. Rereading Liang Fa's tracts in 1843, he concluded that the father was God, the elder brother Jesus Christ, and that he himself was God's second son, called to restore true worship to China. He destroyed Confucian tablets in his village school and began preaching with his cousin Hong Rengan and friend Feng Yunshan.

Feng Yunshan built up the Society of God Worshippers among poor Hakka charcoal burners and farmers in the Thistle Mountain (Zijingshan) region of Guangxi, an area torn by banditry and Hakka–Punti feuds. In 1847 Hong spent some two months in Canton studying with the American Southern Baptist missionary Issachar J. Roberts, who declined to baptise him. In Guangxi, Yang Xiuqing, a charcoal burner, began to speak in trances as the voice of God the Father and Xiao Chaogui as the voice of Jesus, giving them great authority over the movement. Iconoclastic attacks on temples brought conflict with local gentry and militias, and in 1850 the God Worshippers mobilised at Jintian village; in January 1851 Hong proclaimed the Taiping Tianguo, the 'Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace'.

The Taiping army, which separated men and women into different camps and forbade opium, alcohol, gambling and foot-binding, broke out of encirclement at Yong'an in 1852 and marched north through Hunan, gathering hundreds of thousands of followers. Feng Yunshan and Xiao Chaogui were killed in 1852, but the Taiping took Wuchang in January 1853 and Nanjing in March 1853, slaughtering the Manchu garrison and many of its dependants. Renamed Tianjing, the Heavenly Capital, Nanjing became the seat of a theocratic state that printed its own edition of the Bible (based on Karl Gützlaff's translation), enforced the Ten Commandments, held examinations on Taiping scripture and proclaimed an egalitarian, though never implemented, land system. A Northern Expedition sent against Beijing in 1853 reached the outskirts of Tianjin before being destroyed in 1855.

In 1856 the movement tore itself apart in the Tianjing Incident. Yang Xiuqing, speaking as God the Father, demanded equal title with Hong, who then had him killed by the North King Wei Changhui; Wei's troops massacred thousands of Yang's followers before Wei himself was executed. Shi Dakai, the most respected general, left Nanjing with a large army in 1857 and fought on independently until his capture and execution in Sichuan in 1863. Hong withdrew into his palace. The arrival of Hong Rengan in 1859, who had worked with Western missionaries in Hong Kong, brought a programme of modernising reforms, and the generals Li Xiucheng and Chen Yucheng won major victories, taking Suzhou in 1860.

The Qing regular armies proved unable to defeat the Taiping, and the dynasty came to depend on new regional forces raised by Confucian scholar-officials, above all Zeng Guofan's Hunan (Xiang) Army, which presented its campaign as a defence of Confucian civilisation against a foreign, blasphemous creed. After the Anglo-French occupation of Beijing and the Convention of Peking in 1860, the Western powers, at first officially neutral and partly sympathetic to rebels who professed Christianity, decided to support the Qing. They defended Shanghai, and the 'Ever Victorious Army', commanded by the American Frederick Townsend Ward and then by the British officer Charles Gordon, fought alongside Li Hongzhang's Huai Army. Zeng Guoquan captured Anqing in 1861, where much of the population was massacred, and then besieged Nanjing. At Suzhou in December 1863 Li Hongzhang had the surrendered Taiping kings executed in breach of Gordon's assurances.

Hong Xiuquan died in Nanjing on 1 June 1864, probably from illness, after urging his followers to eat 'manna'. On 19 July 1864 Zeng Guoquan's troops broke into the city, and in the days that followed a vast number of Taiping soldiers and civilians were killed; Zeng Guofan reported that more than 100,000 had died. Hong's teenage son was captured and executed, and Li Xiucheng wrote a long confession before his execution. Taiping remnants fought on in the south until 1866, while the related Nian rebellion and Muslim risings in the north-west continued for years.

The war devastated the lower Yangzi, China's richest region, and shifted military and fiscal power from the court to regional leaders such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, who went on to lead the Self-Strengthening Movement. Sun Yat-sen admired Hong as an anti-Manchu revolutionary, and the People's Republic later honoured the Taiping as a peasant revolution. For Protestant missions, the rebellion was an embarrassing demonstration of how the Christian message could be transformed when separated from church teaching, and it deepened Chinese official suspicion of Christianity as subversive.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/nameOfGod: Hong Xiuquan proclaimed that God the Heavenly Father (Shangdi, the ancient Chinese name for the Supreme Lord, used in Protestant tracts) had sent him, as Jesus' younger brother, to destroy the demons and establish a kingdom of heaven on earth. Manchus were described as 'demons' and 'imps', and idols, Buddhist and Daoist temples and Confucian tablets were smashed as demonic. Taiping soldiers prayed before meals and battles, kept the Sabbath, sang doxologies and memorised the Ten Commandments and Taiping odes; offences against the commandments, including adultery and opium smoking, were punishable by death. Yang Xiuqing's trances as the voice of God the Father gave divine sanction to commands and executions. On the Qing side, Zeng Guofan's 1854 proclamation against the rebels called scholars to defend the Confucian moral order and the gods of China against a religion that, he wrote, overturned the relations of ruler and subject, father and son.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/religiousCau: Hong Xiuquan's visions and his reading of Liang Fa's Protestant tracts convinced him that he was God's son with a mission to rule China and destroy idolatry.
The God Worshippers' iconoclasm against temples and images brought them into armed conflict with local gentry and militias in Guangxi.
The movement's theology identified the Manchu rulers and their officials as demons who had usurped worship due to God alone.
Trance revelations by Yang Xiuqing and Xiao Chaogui gave the movement a charismatic, prophetic leadership demanding obedience.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/otherCauses/: Population pressure, land shortage, floods and famine created mass poverty in southern China in the 1840s.
The Opium War (1839–42) humiliated the Qing, disrupted trade routes and left unemployed labourers and boatmen around Guangzhou.
Hakka–Punti ethnic conflict in Guangxi drove Hakka communities to seek protection in the God Worshippers.
Han Chinese resentment of Manchu rule and of corrupt officials gave the revolt a powerful ethnic and political appeal.
The weakness of the Qing banner and Green Standard armies allowed the rebellion to expand rapidly.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/triggers/0: Clashes between the God Worshippers and local militias in Guangxi in 1850.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/triggers/1: The mobilisation at Jintian and Hong's proclamation of the Heavenly Kingdom on 11 January 1851.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/triggers/2: The God Worshippers' defeat of Qing troops sent against them at Jintian in late 1850 and early 1851, which committed the movement to open war.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/0/t: Hong Xiuquan receives Liang Fa's tracts in Guangzhou.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/1/t: Hong's visions after his third examination failure.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/2/t: Hong interprets his visions through the tracts and begins preaching.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/3/t: Hong studies with Issachar Roberts in Canton; the God Worshippers grow in Guangxi.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/4/t: Proclamation of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom at Jintian; kings appointed at Yong'an.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/5/t: Taiping capture Nanjing and make it the Heavenly Capital; Northern Expedition launched.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/6/t: The Northern Expedition is destroyed near Tianjin and in Shandong.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/7/t: Tianjing Incident: Yang Xiuqing and thousands of his followers killed.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/8/t: Hong Rengan arrives in Nanjing and becomes chief minister.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/9/t: Taiping take Suzhou and threaten Shanghai; Roberts visits Nanjing.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/11/: Suzhou surrenders; Li Hongzhang executes the Taiping kings; Shi Dakai captured in Sichuan.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/12/: Hong Xiuquan dies; Nanjing falls on 19 July with mass killings.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/timeline/13/: Last Taiping armies are destroyed in the south.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/0/: Heavenly King of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
Founded the movement on his visions, claimed to be God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus, and ruled from Nanjing as a theocratic monarch.
Died in Nanjing in June 1864 shortly before its fall; later claimed as a revolutionary ancestor by both Nationalists and Communists.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/1/: South King and organiser of the God Worshippers
Built the God Worshipping Society in Guangxi and devised much of its organisation and calendar.
Killed in battle in Hunan in 1852.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/2/: Spoke as the voice of God the Father in trances and became the real administrator of the Taiping state.
Killed in the Tianjing Incident of 1856 when he sought equal status with Hong.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/3/: One of the ablest Taiping commanders; left Nanjing after the 1856 purge and campaigned independently.
Trapped at the Dadu River in Sichuan, surrendered and was executed in 1863.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/4/: Baptised and trained by missionaries in Hong Kong, he proposed railways, banks, newspapers and closer relations with the West in his New Treatise on Political Counsel (1859).
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/5/: Led the Taiping campaigns in the lower Yangzi and against Shanghai and defended Nanjing to the end.
Captured after the fall of Nanjing and executed after writing a long confession.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/6/: A Confucian scholar-official who raised a new regional army and framed the war as a defence of Chinese civilisation against a heterodox religion.
Became the most powerful official in China and a leader of the Self-Strengthening Movement.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/7/: Recaptured the Suzhou region with the Ever Victorious Army and executed the surrendered Taiping kings.
Dominated Qing foreign and military affairs for the rest of the century.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/8/: Taught Hong in 1847 and lived in Nanjing as a guest of the Taiping in 1860–62.
Fled and denounced Hong's regime as murderous and blasphemous; returned to the United States.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/keyPeople/9/: Commander of the Ever Victorious Army
An evangelical British officer who led Qing-paid troops in recapturing Jiangsu towns in 1863–64.
Known thereafter as 'Chinese Gordon'; killed at Khartoum in 1885.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/casualties/n: The figure of 20–30 million dead, from combat, massacre, famine and epidemic disease, is the range most commonly given by historians such as Jonathan Spence and Stephen Platt. Some Chinese demographers, such as Cao Shuji, have estimated population losses in the affected provinces of up to 70 million, but these include reduced births and migration as well as deaths. No reliable count exists, and Qing and Taiping records were partly destroyed.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effects/0: The lower Yangzi region, China's economic heartland, was devastated, and some districts took decades to recover their population.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effects/1: Power shifted from the Manchu court to regional Han Chinese leaders and their personal armies, a trend that contributed to the warlordism of the early twentieth century.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effects/2: Western involvement in defending Shanghai and training Qing forces deepened foreign influence in China.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effects/3: The Qing dynasty survived but was gravely weakened, and the Self-Strengthening Movement grew out of the campaigns against the Taiping.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effects/4: The Taiping became a symbol of revolution for Sun Yat-sen and later Chinese Communist historiography.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/effectsOnChu: The rebellion reinforced Chinese official and gentry suspicion that Christianity was subversive and heterodox, feeding anti-missionary hostility.

Protestant missionaries, initially hopeful that the Taiping would open China to the gospel, became disillusioned, and many concluded that the Bible should not be distributed without teachers and churches.
The widespread Taiping use of Protestant terminology and scripture shaped how Chinese people first encountered Christian language.
Missions expanded after the 1860 treaties, partly in the regions devastated by the war, under the protection of unequal treaties that further linked Christianity with Western power.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/legacy: The Taiping Rebellion is a sobering case of how Christian scriptures, read in isolation and fused with personal visions, ethnic grievance and social despair, could inspire a theocratic movement of extraordinary violence. It remains contested: celebrated in China as a peasant revolution, studied by historians of religion as a new religious movement, and remembered by churches as a warning about the separation of Christian texts from Christian community and teaching.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/dissenters/0: After living in Nanjing, Hong's former teacher wrote in 1862 that the Heavenly King was a madman whose religion was a political sham and whose regime was built on murder, and he urged that the movement be recognised for what it was.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/dissenters/1: The Welsh Congregationalist missionary visited Taiping territory in 1860, met Hong Rengan and pressed the leaders on Christian doctrine, rejecting Hong's claims to divine sonship while hoping to correct the movement's teaching.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/dissenters/2: Though fighting for the Qing, Gordon was so outraged by Li Hongzhang's execution of the Taiping kings who had surrendered at Suzhou in 1863 that he temporarily withdrew his troops and refused imperial rewards.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/theatres/0/n: Jintian, proclamation of the Heavenly Kingdom
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/theatres/8/n: Surrender of Suzhou and execution of the kings
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/campaigns/0/: The Taiping march from Guangxi to Nanjing
Hong Xiuquan, Yang Xiuqing, Feng Yunshan and the Taiping army

Breaking out of Yong'an in April 1852, the Taiping failed to take Guilin, lost Feng Yunshan near Quanzhou and Xiao Chaogui at Changsha, then seized boats at Yuezhou and swept down the Yangzi, taking Wuchang and Anqing before capturing Nanjing in March 1853.
conflicts/taiping-rebellion/campaigns/1/: A Taiping army marched north through Henan and Shanxi to within reach of Tianjin, but, poorly supplied and unprepared for the northern winter, it was pushed back by the Mongol general Sengge Rinchen and destroyed in Zhili and Shandong in 1855.
